the characteristics of the response of the neurons to an acceleration stimulus were not altered following vestibular nerve transection.
the characteristics of the vestibular-evoked second-order neural response to a sinusoidal acceleration were not significantly altered after contralateral labyrinthectomy.

(a) the resting discharge rate of the neurons is not changed by vestibular nerve section; (b) the maximal response rate to an 8 deg/sec2 acceleration is not changed by section; and (c) the rate of adaptation of the response is not changed by contralateral vestibulotomy.

the effects of contralateral labyrinthectomy on the second-order vestibular system.

the characteristics of the second-order vestibular neuron response to an acceleration are unaffected by the loss of the contralateral labyrinth.

the vestibular nucleus is organized in a manner which is not dependent on the vestibular nerve.

the vestibular nucleus is organized in a mosaic pattern, with some neurons receiving bilateral labyrinthine input and other neurons receiving unilateral labyrinthine input, but with the same type of input to both sides of the brainstem.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the absence of vestibular input, the central nervous system can generate a response to acceleration that resembles the response to acceleration seen in intact animals.
, in general, the vestibular nucleus is capable of maintaining a high level of function after unilateral labyrinthectomy.
